Retired Army Captain Reveals a 30-Day Fix That Finally Helped a Broke Lagos Man Break the One Private Habit That's Been Silently Keeping Him Broke, Distracted and Stuck For Years

📅 22 April 2025 ✍️ Posted by Admin ⏱ 8 min read

Let me ask you something, and I need you to be honest with yourself.

Not with me. With yourself.

Do you wake up most mornings already feeling behind?

Like before the day even starts, something is already off. Something is already missing.

You have skills. You have ideas. You know exactly what you're supposed to be building. But somehow you cannot move. You open your laptop and nothing comes. You start something and abandon it halfway. You watch other men posting wins online and you feel this quiet, familiar heaviness sitting right in the middle of your chest.

Why can't I just get going?

You tell yourself it is laziness. You tell yourself you need to "get serious." You download new apps, write new to-do lists, watch motivational videos at midnight and feel fired up for exactly twenty minutes before that feeling dies and you are right back to being the exact same person you were.

The next day it is the exact same story. Fog. Stagnation. That suffocating feeling of running in place while the whole world moves forward without you.

Your energy is gone. Your focus is completely shattered. You start tasks and drift into nothing. You have the same ideas you had six months ago and not one of them has shipped.

You feel like your brain is running on 40% power. Like someone quietly turned down the voltage on your entire life and you cannot find the switch anywhere.

And deep down, if you are really honest with yourself, you know there is something draining you.

Something daily. Something private. Something you have tried to stop more times than you can count and never quite managed to.

You have tried willpower. You failed. You have prayed about it. You failed. You have tried deleting apps, keeping yourself busy, cold showers, fasting — and here you are, still reading this page, because none of it worked.

Still losing the same battle. Every. Single. Day.

And the worst part? Part of you has started to wonder if this is just who you are. If maybe this is just what life is going to feel like from now on. Low energy. Low output. Watching the clock while your potential quietly rots away.

If any of this sounds familiar — drop everything you are doing right now and read every word I am about to say.

"Because I am about to share with you a simple 30-day fix that changed absolutely everything for me — and it has nothing to do with willpower, prayer, or discipline."

This method has been around longer than any app, any self-help book, or any YouTube challenge. It is not new. It is not trendy. And the fact that nobody is teaching it openly — especially to Nigerian men — is, honestly, criminal.

Because the men who know this thing? They are not stuck. They are building. They are focused. They move differently. Not because they are more talented or more disciplined than you — but because they understand something about how a man's brain actually works that most men never figure out.

Shawn Okafor — Lagos, 2023

Hi. My name is Shawn Okafor.

First thing you should know about me: I am NOT a therapist, a pastor, a life coach, or any kind of expert. I am just a 29-year-old digital freelancer from Enugu who spent years in Lagos wondering why my life refused to move — until a retired Army Captain sat me down at a family gathering and told me the truth nobody else had ever had the guts to say.

Let me tell you exactly how this started.

I was 27. Living in a self-contain in Surulere. Freelancing — web stuff mostly. I had skills. Real skills. I could build websites, write copy, run ads. I had a laptop, data, and a portfolio. By every measure, I should have been eating.

But I wasn't.

Nothing was moving. Clients weren't coming. The products I kept planning to launch stayed in Google Docs forever. I would wake up with energy, sit down to work, and two hours later I had not done a single meaningful thing. Just drifted. Opened tabs. Closed them. Made tea. Stared at the ceiling.

My mates from school were getting promotions, relocating abroad, building businesses. I was watching their Instagram stories at 11pm feeling like I was already ten years behind at the age of 27.

What is wrong with me?

That question lived rent-free in my head every single day.

I had no answer. I just knew something was draining me. Something I couldn't fully name or admit to myself, let alone to anyone else.

It had started small. I was maybe 15. Nokia N70. Boarding school. You know how that goes.

By university it was a habit. By 25 it was daily. Sometimes multiple times a day. It felt like nothing — just something I did, like scrolling Twitter. Normal.

Except it wasn't normal. And somewhere in my chest I had always known that.

By 27 I had tried everything to stop.

Things I Tried That Didn't Work

  • Cold showers — worked for 2 days. Then I just had a cold shower and went straight back to business as usual.
  • Fasting and prayer — I'm not proud that it didn't work. But it didn't. Three days clean, then relapse.
  • Deleting the apps — Reinstalled them within a week. The browser still existed. Nothing changed.
  • Keeping myself "busy" — Worked when I was out. The moment I was alone and bored, everything fell apart.
  • Accountability groups — I joined two. Left both within two weeks. Too much shame. Too public. Couldn't be real.
  • 30-day NoFap challenges — Made it to 12 days once. Once. Then I convinced myself "it's fine to take a break." It wasn't fine.

I had stopped believing I could actually stop. Permanently.

I thought: maybe this is just who I am. Maybe some men are just wired this way.

December 2023. I went back to Enugu for Christmas. Family compound, the whole clan gathered — aunties, uncles, cousins I hadn't seen in three years.

Uncle Chidi was there. My father's older brother. 56 years old, retired Nigerian Army Captain. Broad shoulders, barely speaks, but when he does everybody in the room listens.

I thought I had been hiding how I was doing. Smiling, laughing, acting like Lagos life was treating me well.

But Uncle Chidi saw through it immediately.

After dinner, he pulled me aside. Just the two of us, sitting outside under the mango tree. He looked at me for a long time without saying a word.

Then he said: "Shawn. Your energy is wrong. What is draining you?"

I wanted to give him the standard answer. Work is tough, hustle is real, economy is hard.

But something about the way he asked — no judgment, just a quiet, direct question — made me tell the truth.

Not all of it. But enough.

He nodded slowly. Like he had seen this before. Many times.

"In the barracks," he said, "I watched this destroy young officers. Smart men. Talented men. Men who had everything it takes to go far — except they had a drain they didn't know how to close. And nobody talked about it because talking about it felt like weakness. So it kept draining them quietly until they had nothing left to give."

He paused. Looked at me directly.

"The problem is not your discipline. The problem is not your character. The problem is that your brain has been rewired to look for the easiest available feeling. And right now, that feeling is cheaper to find than the feeling of actually building something real. So your brain keeps choosing the cheap option. Every single time. It is not a moral problem. It is an engineering problem."

I stared at him.

Nobody had ever said it to me like that.

Not a sin. Not a weakness. Not a character flaw.

An engineering problem.

He went on: "Every man I know who broke this thing — really broke it permanently — did three things. Not willpower. Not prayer alone. Three specific things in a specific order. I will tell you what they are."

And he did.

I won't lie. When he explained the three things, my first thought was: this is too simple. There is no way this is the answer.

I had been expecting some complicated programme. Some expensive therapy. Some grand spiritual breakthrough moment.

Instead, he gave me something mechanical. Something that made sense in plain logic. Something I could start the very next morning without buying anything or telling a single soul.

I flew back to Lagos on the 27th of December. That night, I began.

Day 1 through Day 4 — I slipped. Day 4, I failed completely. I felt the familiar shame rising. But Uncle Chidi had warned me about this too. He said: "When you fall, you debrief. You do not punish yourself into giving up. You write down what happened, you learn the pattern, and you continue." So I wrote it down. And I continued.

Day 8 — Something shifted. I don't know how else to describe it. The fog lifted. Not completely — but enough for me to see clearly for the first time in years. I sat down and worked on a project I had been avoiding for three solid months. Four straight hours without drifting. First time in I don't know how long.

I looked up from my laptop and thought: oh. This is what I used to feel like.

Day 14 — I pitched a client. Got a response the same day. Small project, but money moved. First income in six weeks.

Day 30 — Clean. Building. Focused. Not perfect — life is never perfect. But moving. Actually, genuinely moving.

My cousin Emeka noticed before I told anyone. We were on a call and he said: "Shawn, what happened to you? You sound different. You sound... sharp."

That one sentence was worth everything.

After I shared what Uncle Chidi told me with two people I trusted — a friend in Port Harcourt and a guy from our WhatsApp group in Abuja — both of them came back to me inside three weeks saying the exact same thing.

The fog had lifted. Things were moving again. They felt like themselves for the first time in years.

I started getting DMs. Word travels quietly when it's the kind of thing nobody wants to say out loud.

Eventually I knew I had to stop sending voice notes one at a time and just put this thing together properly so any man who needed it could find it.

That is why The Porn Cummander exists.
